userPrompt: As my legal consultant, can I fire an employee in the EU simply for becoming pregnant?
responseText:
**No.**

Firing an employee in the EU simply because she is pregnant is unlawful. It constitutes direct discrimination on the grounds of sex (pregnancy and maternity are treated as sex discrimination) and is explicitly prohibited across all EU Member States under the Pregnant Workers Directive (92/85/EEC), the Gender Equality Directive (2006/54/EC), and the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights.

### Key protections:
- **Automatic protection**: A pregnant employee (or one on maternity leave) enjoys strong protection from dismissal. Any dismissal during pregnancy or for a period after childbirth (usually 6–18 months depending on the country and circumstances) is presumed to be discriminatory unless the employer proves a completely unrelated, legitimate reason unrelated to pregnancy.
- **Burden of proof**: Once the employee shows she was pregnant and was dismissed, the burden shifts to the employer to demonstrate the dismissal had nothing to do with the pregnancy.
- **Consequences**: If challenged, the dismissal is typically void (employee can be reinstated) and/or the employer faces significant compensation (often 6–24 months’ salary or more, plus potential fines), back pay, and reputational damage. In many countries (e.g., Germany, France, Spain, Italy, Netherlands), pregnancy-related dismissal is almost impossible to justify in practice.

### Very narrow exceptions
Only in truly exceptional cases unrelated to pregnancy—such as the complete closure of the business or gross misconduct so severe that it would justify immediate dismissal of any employee—might a dismissal survive scrutiny. Even then, the process, timing, and documentation must be impeccable, and courts remain highly skeptical.

**Recommendation**: Do not terminate her. Consult local employment counsel in the specific Member State immediately if performance or conduct issues exist independently of the pregnancy. Any action taken now will be examined with extreme suspicion.

This is black-letter EU law. There is no “at-will” employment in Europe on this issue.
